strengths: The paper addresses an important object in deep learning and information geometry: estimating and bounding the Fisher information metric for classifier networks.

The decomposition through the low-dimensional simplex/core space is clean and gives a useful way to relate spectral properties of the categorical Fisher matrix to the neural-network Fisher via the logits Jacobian.

The Hutchinson-style estimator is simple, architecture-agnostic, unbiased, and practically implementable with automatic differentiation; the variance analysis for diagonal entries is a useful sanity guarantee.
The manuscript is generally readable and includes detailed proofs in the appendix.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main random estimator is essentially the standard identity that for a Gram/Fisher matrix F = AA^T, drawing a random probe xi and forming A xi xi^T A^T gives an unbiased rank-one matrix estimator. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from existing randomized sketching, Fisher trace, and stochastic natural-gradient literature.

The empirical evaluation is far below the bar for the paper’s practical claims. It only shows density plots on DistilBERT for small batches/datasets, with no quantitative error against exact or high-sample Fisher estimates, no runtime or memory comparison, no downstream optimizer/application, and no comparison to KFAC, MC Fisher estimators, BackPACK-style methods, or other established approximations.

Several claims are overstated. The estimator is described as efficient for full, block-diagonal, or diagonal Fisher estimation, but a single rank-one sample does not provide a useful full-rank Fisher estimate without many probes, and storing or using the full outer product remains infeasible for large networks.

The deterministic bounds are mathematically interesting but their practical utility is not demonstrated. The paper does not show when the lower/upper bounds are tight in realistic settings, how many power iterations are needed, or whether the bounds improve any actual algorithmic decision.

The computational-cost discussion is incomplete: summing over all classes in the proposed scalar h can be expensive for large output spaces, and the paper compares this to full-class losses rather than common sampled or label-only training losses.

Reproducibility is weak: no code, implementation details, hyperparameters, exact preprocessing, seeds, or sufficient experimental protocol are provided. The experiments appear more illustrative than evidential.

Some notation and presentation issues reduce confidence, including overloaded symbols for empirical and Monte Carlo Fisher estimates, occasional orientation inconsistencies in Jacobian/gradient products, and claims such as bounded coefficient of variation that need more careful qualification near zero Fisher entries.

strengths: The paper studies an important object: the Fisher information matrix for classification networks, and connects the network-level FIM to the low-dimensional simplex metric via a pullback/Gauss-Newton form.
Some of the deterministic spectral observations for the categorical simplex, such as the diag(p)-pp^T structure and Loewner upper/lower bounds, are clearly presented and may be useful pedagogically.
The proposed random-sign estimator is simple to implement with automatic differentiation and gives an unbiased rank-one estimate of the FIM when summing over the full dataset/classes.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The Hutchinson-style construction is essentially a randomized sketch of a Fisher square-root/Jacobian factor, and the relationship to existing stochastic Fisher, Jacobian sketching, natural-gradient, and trace-estimation literature is not positioned convincingly enough to support a top-tier contribution.

The main quality guarantee is weak and overstated. A bounded coefficient of variation for individual diagonal entries, roughly sqrt(2), still implies very noisy single-sample estimates, and the paper does not provide meaningful high-probability, matrix-norm, optimization-relevant, or downstream guarantees.

The comparison to Monte Carlo estimators is not fair. The paper contrasts a full-dataset Hutchinson estimator against MC estimators that include data-sampling variance; if the proposed estimator is used on minibatches, the same data-distribution/heavy-tail issues can reappear.

The empirical evaluation is far too thin. It consists mainly of density plots for DistilBERT on small batches/datasets, with no optimizer experiment, no downstream performance, no runtime/memory analysis, no scaling to large class counts, no comparison to KFAC/diagonal Fisher/BackPACK-style baselines, and no validation that the estimator improves any practical use case.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. Statements such as practical scalability, universal applicability, and guaranteed quality are not supported for full matrices, block diagonals, large-output problems, or realistic training workflows.

Some theoretical parts appear either routine or of unclear utility. The deterministic bounds often require quantities such as Jacobian singular values or leading simplex eigenvectors and may be expensive or loose in the regimes where they would be useful.

There are possible technical issues in the proofs and assumptions, especially around bounds involving J^T A J and smallest singular values, rank/full-row-rank conditions, and transitions from core-space bounds to network-space statements. These need much more careful treatment.

The paper itself concedes that thorough numerical experiments and real applications, such as a new optimizer, are left for future work. For a top-tier AI venue, this leaves the contribution under-evidenced and largely conceptual.
Reproducibility is limited: the experiments are small, implementation details are sparse, and there is no released code or sufficiently detailed protocol for reproducing the estimator comparisons.

strengths: The paper studies an important and practically relevant object: Fisher/metric tensors for classifier networks, where exact computation is usually infeasible but approximations are central to optimization, uncertainty, and geometry-based analysis.

The core technical idea is clean: analyze the low-dimensional simplex FIM, transfer deterministic Loewner/Frobenius-type bounds through the network Jacobian, and use Hutchinson-style randomization to obtain unbiased FIM estimators computable by automatic differentiation.

The Hutchinson estimator is simple and potentially useful in practice: it avoids sampling labels one by one, can be implemented with detach-style operations, and gives clear variance/CV guarantees for diagonal entries.

The paper is mathematically coherent overall, with most claims accompanied by appendix proofs. The distinction among empirical FIM, Monte Carlo FIM, deterministic bounds, and Hutchinson estimates is useful and helps position the contribution.

The work provides some empirical intuition on DistilBERT, including both an untrained classification-head setting and a fine-tuned SST-2 setting, showing the relative scale of the proposed lower/upper estimates and empirical FIM.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is quite thin for a top-tier AI venue. The experiments are mainly density visualizations on DistilBERT and do not quantitatively compare accuracy, variance, runtime, memory, convergence behavior, or downstream utility against MC Fisher, empirical Fisher, KFAC, diagonal Fisher estimators, BackPACK-style tools, or natural-gradient approximations.

The practical significance remains under-demonstrated. The conclusion explicitly leaves optimizers and real applications for future work, so the paper’s impact depends heavily on theoretical elegance rather than demonstrated benefit in learning or analysis workflows.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence. The estimator is called guaranteed-quality, but the most concrete variance guarantee is for individual diagonal entries; a single rank-1 full-matrix sample can have very high variance and insufficient rank, and the paper does not fully characterize practical sample complexity for block/full tensor use.

The deterministic lower-bound estimator requires computing the top eigenpair of the simplex FIM per sample and still involves Jacobian-vector/backward computations; the paper does not convincingly benchmark whether this is worthwhile relative to simpler alternatives.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: Hutchinson randomization and Fisher/trace estimation are well known, and the estimator follows naturally from writing the Fisher as a sum of outer products. The paper’s contribution is a useful synthesis and analysis, but not clearly a major conceptual leap.
The numerical section lacks reproducibility details such as code, exact estimator implementation, random seeds, wall-clock costs, and statistical variability across runs or sample counts.

There are presentation and rigor issues in places: notation is occasionally overloaded, some proofs use terse matrix-inequality steps that would benefit from additional conditions or clarification, and the paper would be stronger with explicit assumptions on Jacobian rank, dataset sampling, and parameter dimensions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important object in deep learning and information geometry: estimating the Fisher information matrix/metric tensor for classifier networks at scale.
The decomposition through the low-dimensional probability simplex is clean, and several deterministic upper/lower bounds are derived from interpretable spectral properties of the simplex FIM.
The Hutchinson-style estimator is simple to implement with automatic differentiation, unbiased for the FIM, and has a clear per-coordinate variance bound for diagonal entries.

The empirical section covers multiple modalities and model families, and the reported diagonal-FIM errors suggest the proposed estimator can be more accurate than empirical Fisher under comparable single-backward-pass budgets.
weaknesses: The novelty of the main stochastic estimator is not fully convincing: it is essentially a randomized outer-product estimator for a sum of gradient outer products, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish it from existing randomized GGN/Fisher/BackPACK-style estimators beyond terminology.

The evaluation is too limited for a top-tier acceptance: it focuses almost entirely on diagonal FIM estimation error, without showing downstream value for optimization, pruning, continual learning, sharpness, or any application where better FIM estimates materially change outcomes.

Experimental reporting lacks important reproducibility and statistical detail: no code, no confidence intervals over random probes/seeds, limited hyperparameter/runtime detail, and no analysis of sensitivity to number of probes, batch count, class count, or power-iteration budget.

Some baselines are missing or dismissed too quickly. In particular, exact/approximate diagonal GGN/Fisher tooling and stronger Monte Carlo variants should be compared under matched compute, memory, and accuracy tradeoffs.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper claims production practicality and broadly guaranteed quality, but the variance guarantee is mainly per diagonal entry conditional on fixed data and does not establish useful accuracy for the full matrix or downstream algorithms.

There are technical presentation issues and possible errors. For example, Lemma 3 appears to state an upper bound involving 1 - ||p|| - p_(C-1), while the proof uses 1 - ||p||^2 - p_(C-1); as written the bound can be negative. The binary MC variance derivation also appears to have a constant-factor mistake.

The deterministic bounds are mathematically interesting but their practical role is unclear: the paper does not show that using these bounds yields better algorithms, diagnostics, or reliable approximations beyond the reported diagonal-error table.

Scalability claims are qualified: the estimator requires summing over all classes/logits and low-rank variants require eigendecomposition or power iteration over the core, which may be problematic for very large output spaces, but this regime is not evaluated.

strengths: The manuscript is clearly motivated by an important object in deep learning and information geometry: estimating the Fisher information matrix for modern classifiers.

The paper contains several concrete theoretical statements, including spectral bounds for the categorical simplex FIM, deterministic upper/lower bounds after pullback through the network Jacobian, and variance calculations for the proposed random estimators.

The Hutchinson-style construction is computationally simple and potentially useful: it gives an unbiased estimator whose diagonal entries have a bounded coefficient of variation, and it can be implemented with one additional backward pass.
The empirical section covers multiple model families and modalities, including transformer, vision, and speech models, rather than relying on a single toy setting.
weaknesses: The novelty is not convincing enough for a top-tier AI venue. The proposed estimator is essentially a random-feature/Hutchinson estimator for a Gram/Fisher matrix, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish it from known stochastic Fisher, score-function, randomized numerical linear algebra, or automatic-differentiation constructions.

The deterministic bounds are mathematically plausible but their practical significance is unclear. Many results follow from standard properties of categorical covariance matrices, interlacing, Loewner order, and pullbacks; the paper does not show that these bounds enable a new algorithm or materially change practice.

The evaluation is too narrow for the strength of the claims. It only evaluates diagonal FIM estimation accuracy on fixed subsets and does not demonstrate downstream benefit for natural-gradient optimization, pruning, continual learning, regularization, uncertainty, or any other stated use case of the FIM.

Important baselines are missing or dismissed too quickly. The Monte Carlo estimator is excluded from the main comparison due to cost, but the paper does not provide a careful accuracy-compute frontier, multi-sample comparisons, variance-reduction baselines, BackPACK-style estimators, KFAC/block-diagonal approximations, or stronger empirical Fisher alternatives.

The empirical protocol is under-specified. It is unclear how many Hutchinson probes or random seeds are used, how stable the reported RelMAE values are, whether confidence intervals are computed, and how sensitive results are to batch count, batch size, class count, model calibration, or fine-tuning status.

The main table raises questions that are not adequately analyzed. Some methods have enormous errors on certain tasks while others are close, but the paper gives only high-level explanations and no diagnostic analysis of when the proposed estimator fails, when low-rank cores help, or how the error distribution varies across layers and parameter groups.

The claimed production practicality is not fully supported. Computing a full rank-1 outer product is infeasible for large models, so the paper effectively evaluates diagonal or block statistics, but the presentation sometimes speaks as if the full FIM estimator is broadly practical.

Reproducibility is limited: no code, implementation details, hardware-time measurements beyond relative speedups, random seed information, or confidence intervals are provided, and the ground-truth computation procedure is expensive and only performed on small subsets.

The paper acknowledges the absence of downstream integration as a limitation, but this is a major weakness rather than a minor future-work item. Without showing that better FIM estimates improve an actual AI workflow, the contribution remains mostly a theoretical/diagnostic exercise.

Overall, the paper is technically coherent and has some useful observations, but the combination of limited novelty, incomplete empirical validation, missing practical demonstrations, and insufficient reproducibility makes it not competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and technically relevant problem: estimating Fisher information metric tensors for modern classifiers with better guarantees than empirical Fisher or naive Monte Carlo estimates.

The theoretical development is substantial. The analysis of the simplex/core-space FIM, deterministic lower and upper bounds, and variance guarantees for the Hutchinson-style estimator are clearly connected and mostly well motivated.

The proposed estimator is simple and practical: it can be implemented through standard automatic differentiation with roughly one additional backward pass, making the contribution potentially useful for large models.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many theory-heavy submissions, spanning NLP, vision, and audio models, including DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet, EfficientNet, and Wav2Vec2. The reported RelMAE improvements over empirical Fisher are convincing for diagonal FIM estimation.
The paper is generally well organized, with proofs included and a useful comparison between unbiased Hutchinson estimates, empirical Fisher, diagonal-core estimates, and low-rank-core estimates.
weaknesses: The practical impact is not fully demonstrated. The paper estimates Fisher quantities but does not integrate the estimator into downstream uses such as natural-gradient optimization, pruning, continual learning, regularization, or uncertainty estimation, which makes the significance somewhat indirect.

The empirical validation focuses almost entirely on diagonal FIM entries. Although the method is presented as an estimator of the full metric tensor, the experiments do not convincingly evaluate full-matrix or structured approximations where correlations matter.

Novelty should be positioned more carefully. Randomized output-space sketches of Fisher/Gauss-Newton quantities and related BackPACK-style estimators are close in spirit, and the paper could do more to distinguish the proposed estimator from existing randomized curvature/Fisher approximations.

The experimental setup uses fixed subsets and ground truth computed on limited batches. This is understandable computationally, but it leaves open how stable the reported advantages are across seeds, larger data subsets, training stages, and model scales.

Several claims are phrased broadly, such as being a universal estimator or advancing the state of the art, while the evidence is narrower: classification settings, mostly diagonal estimates, and no demonstrated downstream learning benefit.

Some implementation details needed for reproducibility are thin, including exact timing methodology, hardware-normalized costs, variance across runs, memory usage, and whether code/checkpoints will be released.
